entries.what_it_does: Returns or logs an underlying error unchanged (or via fmt.Errorf without %w) instead of wrapping it with call-site context.
entries.why_is_this_bad: Losing the call-site context — and the ability to unwrap/match the original error with errors.Is/errors.As — makes failures hard to diagnose and breaks programmatic error handling further up the call chain.

entries.what_it_does: Treats a nilable return value as the primary success signal instead of checking the accompanying error value first.
entries.why_is_this_bad: Go's idiom is that `err != nil` is the authoritative failure signal; checking the value's nilness first can read a stale or zero value as though it were valid data.

entries.what_it_does: Starts a goroutine that blocks on a channel or waits with no cancellation path, so it never returns.
entries.why_is_this_bad: A goroutine with no way to exit accumulates for the life of the process, leaking memory and, if it holds a lock or connection, exhausting resources.

entries.what_it_does: Closes or releases a resource (file, lock, response body) with an explicit call right before every return path instead of a single deferred call right after acquisition.
entries.why_is_this_bad: Manual cleanup repeated before each return is easy to miss on an early-return or panic path, leaking the resource; `defer` ties release to the enclosing function's lifetime unconditionally.

entries.what_it_does: Appends to a slice obtained by re-slicing another slice (e.g. `s[:n]`) and assumes the result is independent, when both share the same backing array.
entries.why_is_this_bad: Because append reuses the backing array when capacity allows, writes through the new slice can silently corrupt elements still visible through the original slice.
entries.use_instead: b := append([]int(nil), a[:2]...) // copies into a fresh backing array

entries.what_it_does: Relies on an implicit compile-time check only at the call site (or omits one entirely) to confirm a type implements an interface, instead of asserting it directly where the type is defined.
entries.why_is_this_bad: Without a `var _ Interface = (*Type)(nil)` assertion, a signature drift (renamed or retyped method) silently breaks the implementation and the compiler error surfaces far away, at whatever call site first needed the interface.

entries.what_it_does: Writes a near-duplicate test function per input case instead of one test function iterating a table of cases.
entries.why_is_this_bad: Duplicated test functions drift out of sync as the behavior under test evolves, and adding a new case means copy-pasting a whole function instead of appending one table row.
entries.example:
func TestAddPositive(t *testing.T) { if Add(2, 3) != 5 { t.Fail() } }
func TestAddNegative(t *testing.T) { if Add(-2, -3) != -5 { t.Fail() } }

entries.what_it_does: Starts a new context.Background()/context.TODO() (or drops the incoming ctx) partway down a call chain instead of threading the caller's context.Context through.
entries.why_is_this_bad: A dropped context breaks cancellation and deadline propagation from the caller, so a client timeout or shutdown no longer stops the in-flight work downstream.

entries.what_it_does: Adds an explicit constructor or initializer for a type whose zero value is already meaningful and ready to use (e.g. sync.Mutex, bytes.Buffer, a struct of only zero-valued fields).
entries.why_is_this_bad: An unnecessary constructor adds ceremony and a second way to create the type, inviting a caller to construct a zero-value instance manually anyway — Go's contract is that `var t T` should already work.

entries.what_it_does: Mixes value and pointer receivers across a type's method set, or defaults to value receivers on a type that must mutate itself or is expensive to copy.
entries.why_is_this_bad: A mixed method set makes the type satisfy interfaces inconsistently depending on whether a pointer or value is in hand, and value receivers on a mutating struct silently operate on a copy instead of the caller's instance.
entries.example:
type Counter struct { n int }
func (c Counter) Inc() { c.n++ } // mutates a copy, caller's n is unchanged
